### 6.3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

We first observe that the argument in [10, Theorems 3.1 and 4.2] reduces the nilsequence discorrelation problem in the range $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$ to an abelian Type II obstruction.

#### Proposition 6.6 (Nilsequence discorrelation up to an abelian Type II obstruction).

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $d,D,A\geqslant 1$ . Suppose that

$$ 2\leqslant X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}. $$

Let $G/\Gamma$ be a filtered nilmanifold of degree at most $d$ , dimension at most $D$ , and complexity at most $\log^{A}X$ . Let $F\colon G/\Gamma\to\mathbb{C}$ have zero mean and satisfy

$$ \|F\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\leqslant\log^{A}X, $$

let $g:\mathbb{Z}\to G$ be polynomial, and let

$$ f\in\{\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp},\mu\}. $$

Then

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^{*}\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

unless the following exceptional alternative holds.

There exist $A_{1}=C(d,D,A,\varepsilon)>0$ , an admissible trilinear component $h$ arising from Proposition 6.4(c) and a real number

$$ |T|\leqslant(X/H)^{d+1}\log^{A_{1}}X $$

such that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)n^{iT}\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X, \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)n^{iT}\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X. $$

#### Proof.

We argue by induction on the dimension of $G/\Gamma$ . The zero-dimensional case is immediate, since a function with mean zero on a one-point nilmanifold vanishes.

Choose $C_{0}=C_{0}(d,D,A,\varepsilon)$ sufficiently large. On enlarging $C_{0}$ , we may assume that it dominates all logarithmic powers in Proposition 6.4. Moreover, we may assume that

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}|f(n)|\ll H\log^{C_{0}}X. $$

Indeed, for $f=\mu$ this is immediate, while for $f=\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ it follows from Shiu’s bound and the definition of $\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ . Let $A_{1}$ be sufficiently large in terms of $d,D,A,\varepsilon,C_{0}$ to absorb any logarithmic losses that follow.

Choose $E>A+C_{0}+10$ . By the Fourier decomposition of [10, Proposition 2.9], we have

$$ F=\sum_{\xi\in\Xi}F_{\xi}+O(\log^{-E}X),\qquad|\Xi|+\max_{\xi\in\Xi}\|F_{\xi}\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\ll\log^{O_{d,D,A,E}(1)}X, $$

where $F_{\xi}$ oscillates with central frequency $\xi$ . For each $\xi\in\Xi$ , define

$$ m_{\xi}=\int_{G/\Gamma}F_{\xi},\qquad F_{\xi}^{0}=F_{\xi}-m_{\xi}. $$

Then $F_{\xi}^{0}$ has mean zero; if $\xi\neq 0$ , Haar invariance gives $m_{\xi}=0$ , while the zero-frequency component factors through the quotient by the centre. The error term is controlled by (6.17), the constants $m_{\xi}$ by the major arc estimate of [10, Theorem 3.1(i)], and every component invariant under a positive-dimensional central subgroup by the induction hypothesis on the corresponding quotient. Consequently, after enlarging $A_{1}$ , we may assume, unless the exceptional alternative has already occurred, that $\dim Z(G)=1$ and that $F$ oscillates with a non-zero central frequency.

By Proposition 6.4, the function $f$ can be represented as a linear combination of $O(\log^{O(1)}X)$ functions $h$ of the following forms:

- (i) $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_{1}}X,X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5})$ type I sum;

- (ii) $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_{1}}X,X^{2/5+\varepsilon/5})$ type I2 sum;

- (iii) $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_{1}}X,A_{II}^{-},A_{II}^{+})$ type II sum satisfying (6.18) $\displaystyle X^{2/5}\log^{-O(1)}X\ll A_{II}^{-}\leqslant A_{II}^{+}\ll X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}.$

For $f=\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}$ , the $L^{1}$ error in the last sentence of Proposition 6.4 is smaller than every required logarithmic loss. If the claimed discorrelation estimate fails, we have

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^{*}\gg\frac{H}{\log^{A+1}X}. $$

Then the triangle inequality and the number of components give one function $h$ of one of the above types for which

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^{*}\gg\frac{H}{\log^{A+O(1)}X}. $$

We apply [10, Theorem 4.2] to this component. In the Type I and Type $I_{2}$ cases, and in the non-abelian Type II case, it gives one of the following alternatives:

- Case 1: a non-trivial horizontal character $\eta:G\to\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ of Lipschitz norm $O_{d,D}(\log^{O_{d,D,A,A_{1}}(1)}X)$ satisfies (6.21) $\displaystyle\|\eta\circ g\|_{C^{\infty}[X,X+H]}\ll_{d,D}\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X;$

- Case 2: the component $h$ is Type II and the nilmanifold is abelian.

The size alternative in [10, Theorem 4.2(i),(ii),(iv)] cannot occur. Indeed, the corresponding quantities in the three cases satisfy

$$ X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}=o(H),\qquad X^{1/3}(X^{2/5+\varepsilon/5})^{2/3}=X^{3/5+2\varepsilon/15}=o(H), $$

and, by (6.18),

$$ \max\{A_{II}^{+},X/A_{II}^{-}\}\ll X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}\log^{O(1)}X=o(H). $$

In Case 2, since $\dim Z(G)=1$ , the group $G$ is one-dimensional. The single-frequency property therefore gives

$$ F(g(n)\Gamma)=b\,e(P(n)) $$

for some $b\in\mathbb{C}$ and some polynomial $P:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ of degree at most $d$ . The original failed correlation (6.19) and the component correlation (6.20) give now

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)e(P(n))\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X, \displaystyle\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)e(P(n))\right|^{*} \displaystyle\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_{1}}X. $$

After normalising by $b$ , [10, Theorem 4.2(iii)] gives an integer $q\ll\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X$ and a number $|T|\leqslant(X/H)^{d+1}\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|e(P(n))n^{-iT}\|_{\mathrm{TV}((X,X+H]\cap\mathbb{Z};q)} \displaystyle\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}\log^{O(A_{1})}X, $$

By [10, Lemma 2.2(iii)], combining (6.22) and (6.23) with (6.24) and enlarging $A_{1}$ give (6.15) and (6.16). This is the exceptional alternative in the statement.

Therefore, it remains to consider the case in which (6.21) holds. As in [10, Section 4.2], we apply [10, Lemma 2.11] to factor $g\in\Poly(\mathbb{Z}\to G)$ as $g=\varepsilon g^{\prime}\gamma$ , where $\varepsilon$ is smooth, $\gamma$ is rational and $g^{\prime}\in\Poly(\mathbb{Z},\ker\eta)$ . Freezing $\varepsilon$ and $\gamma$ incurs an error of $O(H\log^{-A-1}X)$ and splits $(X,X+H]$ into $O(\log^{O_{A_{1}}(1)}X)$ arithmetic progressions $P_{j}$ , as in [10, Section 4.2]. On each $P_{j}$ , we are therefore reduced to a nilsequence $F_{j}(g_{j}(n)\Gamma_{j})$ on a proper rational subnilmanifold $G_{j}/\Gamma_{j}$ satisfying $\dim G_{j}<\dim G$ .

With the constants in this factorisation fixed, choose $B^{\prime}$ sufficiently large in terms of $A_{1},A,d,D,\varepsilon$ to absorb the number of progressions and all other logarithmic losses. If the induction hypothesis, applied to the mean-zero part of some $F_{j}$ on the original interval $(X,X+H]$ , yields its exceptional alternative, then it gives (6.15) and (6.16), together with the required bound for $T$ , with a possibly larger logarithmic exponent. We enlarge the final value of $A_{1}$ to that exponent. Otherwise, after subtracting the mean of $F_{j}$ , the major arc estimate and the induction hypothesis, both applied with saving exponent $B^{\prime}$ , give

$$ \Big|\sum_{n\in P_{j}}f(n)F_{j}(g_{j}(n)\Gamma_{j})\Big|^{*}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{B^{\prime}}X}. $$

Intersecting an arbitrary arithmetic progression with the $P_{j}$ and summing the resulting estimates gives

$$ \Big|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\Big|^{*}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

as claimed. This completes the induction and hence the proof. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let $f\in\{\mu,\Lambda-\Lambda_{X}^{\sharp}\}$ . Subtracting the mean of $F$ , the constant part is bounded by [10, Theorem 3.1(i)]; thus we may suppose that $F$ has mean zero. The Lipschitz norm of the new $F$ is at most $2/\delta$ . Fix a sufficiently large $M=M(A,d,D)$ , and write

$$ A^{\prime}=\max\{A,M+1\}. $$

If $\delta<\log^{-M}X$ , the trivial estimate

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right|^{*}\ll\delta^{-1}H\log X $$

is at most $\delta^{-O_{d,D}(1)}H\log^{-A}X$ once the exponent implicit in $O_{d,D}(1)$ is chosen sufficiently large. If $\delta\geqslant\log^{-M}X$ , the complexity of $G/\Gamma$ is at most $\log^{M}X$ . We apply Proposition 6.6 to $\overline{F}$ with $A^{\prime}$ in place of $A$ . We reach

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right|^{*}\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}\frac{H}{\log^{A^{\prime}}X}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{A}X}, $$

unless the alternative of that proposition holds.

It remains to rule out the alternative of Proposition 6.6. Let $h,T$ and $A_{1}$ be as there. We apply Proposition 6.5 with $A_{1}+10$ and $d+2$ in place of $A$ and $B$ and let $C_{2}=C_{2}(A_{1}+10,d+2,\varepsilon)$ be the constant denoted $C_{A}$ there. If

$$ \frac{X}{H}\log^{C_{2}}X\leqslant|T|\leqslant\left(\frac{X}{H}\right)^{d+1}\log^{A_{1}}X, $$

then $|T|\leqslant X^{d+2}$ for all sufficiently large $X$ , and Proposition 6.5 gives

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)n^{iT}\right|^{*}\ll\frac{H}{\log^{A_{1}+10}X}, $$

contradicting (6.16).

Suppose instead that

$$ |T|<\frac{X}{H}\log^{C_{2}}X. $$

Then

$$ \|n^{iT}\|_{\mathrm{TV}((X,X+H]\cap\mathbb{Z})}\ll 1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X<n\leqslant X+H\end{subarray}}|(n+1)^{iT}-n^{iT}|\ll 1+|T|\frac{H}{X}\ll\log^{C_{2}}X. $$

Combining this with (6.15) and [10, Lemma 2.2(iii)], we obtain

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\right|^{*}\gg\frac{H}{\log^{A_{1}+C_{2}}X}. $$

The major arc estimate of [10, Theorem 3.1(i)], applied with saving exponent $A_{1}+C_{2}+1$ , contradicts this. Hence the alternative in Proposition 6.6 cannot occur, and the theorem follows. ∎

## 7. Sums of the Möbius function over short intervals

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 1.4. Let us first give the relevant combinatorial decomposition lemma.

#### Lemma 7.1 (Type I, Type II, Type I/II trichotomy).

Let $\tau\in(0,1/2)$ , let $0\leqslant\eta<1-2\tau$ , and let $k\geqslant 1$ . Let $\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{k}\geqslant 0$ , write $S=\sum_{j\leqslant k}\alpha_{j}$ , and suppose that $|S-1|\leqslant\eta$ . For $J\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}$ write $\alpha_{J}=\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_{j}$ . Then at least one of the following alternatives holds.

- (i) There is an index $j_{0}\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ such that $\alpha_{j_{0}}>\tau$ .

- (ii) There is a partition $\{1,\dotsc,k\}=J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ with $\alpha_{J_{1}},\alpha_{J_{2}}\in[\tau,S-\tau].$

- (iii) There is an index $j_{0}\in\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ and a partition $\{1,\dotsc,k\}=\{j_{0}\}\sqcup J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ such that $S-2\tau<\alpha_{j_{0}}\leqslant\tau$ and, for $r\in\{1,2\}$ , we have

$$ S-2\tau<\alpha_{J_{r}}<\tau. $$

#### Proof.

Assume that (i) and (ii) fail. After discarding zero terms, choose maximal disjoint sets $J_{1},J_{2}\subseteq\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ such that $\alpha_{J_{1}},\alpha_{J_{2}}<\tau$ . Write $J_{0}=\{1,\dotsc,k\}\setminus(J_{1}\cup J_{2})$ .

Let us first show that $|J_{0}|=1$ . Since $S\geqslant 2\tau$ , we have $J_{0}\neq\emptyset$ . Assume for contradiction that there exist distinct $r_{1},r_{2}\in J_{0}$ . By maximality,

$$ \alpha_{J_{1}\cup\{r_{1}\}},\alpha_{J_{2}\cup\{r_{2}\}}\geqslant\tau. $$

Since we are not in case (ii), neither sum lies in $[\tau,S-\tau]$ , so both exceed $S-\tau$ . But then

$$ S\geqslant\alpha_{J_{1}\cup\{r_{1}\}}+\alpha_{J_{2}\cup\{r_{2}\}}>2(S-\tau)\geqslant S, $$

which is a contradiction. Hence $|J_{0}|=1$ , so $J_{0}=\{j_{0}\}$ for some $j_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ .

Since case (i) fails, $\alpha_{j_{0}}\leqslant\tau$ . Moreover, neither $J_{1}$ nor $J_{2}$ is empty, since otherwise $S<2\tau$ . We have

$$ \alpha_{j_{0}}=S-\alpha_{J_{1}}-\alpha_{J_{2}}>S-2\tau, $$

and, for $\{r,s\}=\{1,2\}$ ,

$$ \alpha_{J_{r}}=S-\alpha_{j_{0}}-\alpha_{J_{s}}>S-2\tau. $$

Thus if $(i)$ and $(ii)$ fail, we are indeed in case (iii). ∎

We prove Theorem 1.4 following the overall strategy of Matomäki–Teräväinen [11]. We spell out the reduction from the short interval Möbius sum to a comparison of Dirichlet polynomial components, since this is where the Heath-Brown – Iwaniec type estimate is used.

### 7.1. Ramaré extraction and comparison

Choose parameters

$$ P\coloneqq\exp(\log^{2/3+\eta_{0}}X),\qquad Q\coloneqq X^{1/(\log\log X)^{2}}, $$

where $\eta_{0}>0$ is chosen sufficiently small in terms of $\varepsilon$ , and satisfies $\eta_{0}<\min\{1/40,\varepsilon/2\}$ . Employing a Ramaré-type identity [11, Lemma 3.1] with $2\eta_{0}$ in place of $\varepsilon$ , we obtain, uniformly for $X^{2\eta_{0}}\leqslant H\leqslant X$ ,

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)=-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}X<prn\leqslant X+H\\
P<p\leqslant Q\\
r\leqslant X^{\eta_{0}}\end{subarray}}a_{r}\mu(n)+O\left(H\frac{\log P}{\log Q}\right), $$

with coefficients satisfying $|a_{r}|\leqslant d(r)$ . With the choice (7.1), the error term in (7.2) is $\ll H(\log X)^{-1/3+2\eta_{0}+o(1)}$ , and is therefore $O(H\log^{-1/3+\varepsilon}X)$ by the choice of $\eta_{0}$ .

We next decompose the main term in (7.2). Apply Heath-Brown’s identity [8, (13.38)] to $\mu(n)$ with parameter $K=20$ , and then decompose all variables dyadically. The identity has $2j-1$ variables in its $j$ th summand, and after adjoining dummy variables equal to $1$ , this expresses the main term as a linear combination of $O(\log^{2K+2}X)$ sums of the following form:

$$ S_{\mathcal{I}}\coloneqq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}prn_{1}\cdots n_{2K-1}\in\mathcal{I}\\
p\in(P_{1},2P_{1}],\,r\in(R,2R],n_{j}\in(N_{j},2N_{j}]\\
p\leqslant Q\end{subarray}}a_{r}\alpha_{1}(n_{1})\cdots\alpha_{2K-1}(n_{2K-1}), $$

where $P_{1}\in[P,Q],\,R\in[1/2,X^{\eta_{0}}],\,N_{j}\geqslant 1/2$ , and

$$ P_{1}RN_{1}\cdots N_{2K-1}\asymp X. $$

For $1\leqslant j\leqslant K-1$ , the coefficient $\alpha_{j}(n)$ is an interval indicator (or a dummy factor supported at $1$ , with $N_{j}=1/2$ ); for $K\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$ , it is the Möbius function restricted to an interval with $N_{j}\leqslant(2X)^{1/K}$ (or a dummy factor supported at $1$ , with $N_{j}=1/2$ ). In particular, every factor of length greater than $(2X)^{1/K}$ is a $1$ -weighted factor.

Finally, define

$$ Y\coloneqq X\exp\bigl(-3\log^{1/3}X\bigr). $$

For each dyadic component, we compare the summation over $(X,X+H]$ with the corresponding summation over $(X,X+Y]$ . The required comparison is provided by the following proposition.

#### Proposition 7.2.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ , $B_{0}>0$ , and $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant Y$ . Let $S_{\mathcal{I}}$ be any dyadic component of the form (7.3). Then

$$ S_{(X,X+H]}=\frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]}+O_{\varepsilon,B_{0}}\left(\frac{H}{\log^{B_{0}}X}\right). $$

The estimate is uniform in the dyadic parameters satisfying (7.4).

#### Proof of Theorem 1.4 assuming Proposition 7.2.

If $H>Y$ , the Vinogradov–Korobov estimate for the summatory Möbius function gives

$$ \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)\right|\ll X\exp\bigl(-c\log^{3/5}X(\log\log X)^{-1/5}\bigr)\ll\frac{H}{\log^{100}X}, $$

so there is nothing to prove. We may therefore assume that $H\leqslant Y$ .

Choose $B_{0}=100$ in Proposition 7.2 to compensate for the $O(\log^{2K+2}X)$ dyadic components. Summing (7.6) and recombining Heath-Brown’s identity and (7.2) gives

$$ \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)=\frac{H}{Y}\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+Y}\mu(n)+O_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{H}{\log^{1/3-\varepsilon}X}\right). $$

For some $c>0$ , the main term on the right-hand side is $\ll H\exp(-c\log^{3/5}X(\log\log X)^{-1/5})$ by the classical zero-free region for $\zeta(s)$ , so Theorem 1.4 follows. ∎

### 7.2. The Dirichlet polynomial estimate

We conclude this section with the proof of Proposition 7.2.

There are $O(Y/N_{j_{0}}+1)$ integers $m$ for which one of these holds, and for each of them the difference in the parentheses is $O(1+HN_{j_{0}}/X)=O(HN_{j_{0}}/X)$ . Shiu’s bound for the divisor bounded coefficients $b_{m}$ thus gives

$$ S_{(X,X+H]}-\frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]}\ll\left(\frac{X}{N_{j_{0}}}+\frac{HY}{X}+\frac{HN_{j_{0}}}{X}\right)\log^{O(1)}X. $$

Since $N_{j_{0}}\in(X^{\tau},2X/P]$ , $H\geqslant X^{19/35+\varepsilon}$ , and $Y/X=\exp(-3\log^{1/3}X)$ , this is $\ll_{A,\varepsilon}H/\log^{A}X$ as claimed.

Case 2: Lemma 7.1(ii) or (iii) holds. By a standard reduction using Perron’s formula (see e.g. [5, Lemma 7.2]), it is enough to prove that, for every $A\geqslant 1$ ,

$$ \int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\left|P_{1}(1/2+it)N_{2K}(1/2+it)\prod_{j=1}^{2K-1}N_{j}(1/2+it)\right|\,\textnormal{d}t\ll_{A}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

where

$$ T_{0}=\exp(\log^{1/3}X),\qquad T_{1}=\frac{X^{1+\varepsilon/2}}{H}\leqslant X^{16/35-\varepsilon/2}, $$

and

$$ P_{1}(s)=\sum_{P_{1}<p\leqslant\min\{2P_{1},Q\}}p^{-s},\quad N_{2K}(s)=\sum_{R<r\leqslant 2R}a_{r}r^{-s},\quad N_{j}(s)=\sum_{N_{j}<n\leqslant 2N_{j}}\alpha_{j}(n)n^{-s} $$

for $1\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$ .

Case 2.1: Lemma 7.1(ii) holds. Let $J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}=\{1,\dotsc,2K\}$ be the partition in the lemma and set, for $\ell\in\{1,2\}$ ,

$$ A_{\ell}(s)=\prod_{j\in J_{\ell}}N_{j}(s), $$

and

$$ \beta_{J_{\ell}}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in J_{\ell}}\beta_{j}, $$

so that $A_{\ell}(s)$ has length $X^{\beta_{J_{\ell}}}$ .

Alternative (ii) of Lemma 7.1 gives

$$ \tau\leqslant\beta_{J_{1}},\beta_{J_{2}}\leqslant S-\tau. $$

Since $\tau=\frac{16}{35}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$ ,

$$ T_{1}\leqslant X^{16/35-\varepsilon/2}=X^{\tau-\varepsilon/4}\leqslant\min\{X^{\beta_{J_{1}}},X^{\beta_{J_{2}}}\}. $$

For every $B_{0}>0$ , by the zero-free region estimate in the form used in [11, Lemma 4.3], we have

$$ \sup_{T_{0}\leqslant|t|\leqslant T_{1}}|P_{1}(1/2+it)|\ll_{B_{0}}P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}}X. $$

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, followed by the mean-value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials (see e.g. [8, Theorem 9.1]), (7.10), and (7.4) yields

$$ \displaystyle\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|P_{1}(1/2+it)A_{1}(1/2+it)A_{2}(1/2+it)|\,\,\textnormal{d}t \displaystyle\ll_{B_{0}}P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}}X\left(\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|A_{1}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}|A_{2}(1/2+it)|^{2}\,\,\textnormal{d}t\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\ll P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}}X\left(T_{1}+X^{\beta_{J_{1}}}\right)^{1/2}\left(T_{1}+X^{\beta_{J_{2}}}\right)^{1/2}\log^{O(1)}X \displaystyle\ll P_{1}^{1/2}(X^{\beta_{J_{1}}+\beta_{J_{2}}})^{1/2}\log^{-B_{0}+O(1)}X\ll\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{B_{0}-O(1)}X} $$

Choosing $B_{0}$ sufficiently large therefore gives (7.8).

Case 2.2: Lemma 7.1(iii) holds. Let $\{1,\dotsc,2K\}=\{j_{0}\}\sqcup J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ be the partition in the lemma, and set $\beta_{J_{r}}=\sum_{j\in J_{r}}\beta_{j}$ . Then

$$ S-2\tau<\beta_{j_{0}},\beta_{J_{1}},\beta_{J_{2}}\leqslant\tau. $$

Moreover,

$$ S-2\tau=\frac{3}{35}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}-\rho+O(1/\log X)>\frac{1}{K} $$

for sufficiently large $X$ . Hence $j_{0}\leqslant K-1$ , so $N_{j_{0}}(s)$ is an interval-indicator factor. Absorb $P_{1}(s)$ into either of the other two blocks and subdivide the two product supports into $O_{K}(1)$ dyadic pieces. For a fixed piece, write the product as $L(s)M(s)N(s)$ , with $L(s)=N_{j_{0}}(s)$ , let $L_{0},M_{0},N_{0}$ be the lengths of the polynomials, and set $\widetilde{X}=L_{0}M_{0}N_{0}\asymp_{K}X$ . Writing

$$ L_{0}=\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_{1}},\quad M_{0}=\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_{2}},\quad N_{0}=\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_{3}}, $$

we have $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}\in[\varepsilon/8,16/35-\varepsilon/8]$ with $\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3}=1$ . Furthermore, for sufficiently large $X$ ,

$$ T_{1}\leqslant\widetilde{X}^{16/35-\varepsilon/8},\qquad T_{0}\geqslant\exp(\log^{1/4}\widetilde{X}). $$

Lemma 4.1, applied with $\widetilde{X}$ in place of $X$ and $\varepsilon/8$ in place of $\varepsilon$ , now gives (7.8). ∎

## 8. Computational lemmas

In this section we prove Lemmas 4.2 and 5.2. Note that each of these is a claim about positivity of a piecewise linear function (of the shape $P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)-t-\varepsilon^{10}$ ). A brute force approach would be to check the inequality at all the possible break-points of these functions. Here we provide different proofs, based on looking at slopes of the piecewise linear functions.

Before turning to the proofs of Lemmas 4.2 and 5.2, for $\beta\geqslant\varepsilon$ and $t\in[0,\tau]$ , we define and study the function

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} R_{\beta,\tau}(t)&:=\beta\inf\{\nu\geqslant 0\colon\mathcal{K}(\beta,\nu;\tau)\geqslant t\}\\
&=\max\left\{0,\min\Bigl\{\frac{t}{2},\max\Bigl\{\frac{t-\tau+2\beta}{6},\min\Bigl\{\frac{t-\tau+\frac{8}{5}\beta}{4},\frac{t-\frac{\tau}{2}+\beta}{4}\Bigr\},\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2}\Bigr\}\Bigr\}\right\}.\end{aligned} $$

Splitting into cases, we obtain the following explicit formulas. If $\varepsilon\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau/2$ , then

$$ R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if $0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-2\beta$,}\\
\frac{t-\tau+2\beta}{6},&\text{if $\tau-2\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta$,}\\
\frac{t-\tau+\frac{8}{5}\beta}{4},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$}.\end{cases} $$

If $\tau/2\leqslant\beta\leqslant 5\tau/6$ , then

$$ \displaystyle R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\begin{cases}\frac{t}{2},&\text{if $0\leqslant t\leqslant\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}$,}\\
\frac{t-\tau+2\beta}{6},&\text{if $\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\frac{8}{5}\beta}{4},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{4}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2},&\text{if $\tau-\frac{2}{5}\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$}.\end{cases} $$

If $5\tau/6\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau$ , then

$$ \displaystyle R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\begin{cases}\frac{t}{2},&\text{if $0\leqslant t\leqslant\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}$,}\\
\frac{t-\frac{\tau}{2}+\beta}{4},&\text{if $\beta-\frac{\tau}{2}\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{3\tau}{2}-\beta$},\\
\frac{t-\tau+\beta}{2},&\text{if $\frac{3\tau}{2}-\beta\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$}.\end{cases} $$

Finally, if $\beta>\tau$ , then

$$ R_{\beta,\tau}(t)=\frac{t}{2}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 4.2.

First of all, we observe that $H_{j,\tau}(\nu)$ is nondecreasing in $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ . As a consequence, $\{\nu:H_{j,\tau}(\nu)\geqslant t\}\subseteq\{\nu:H_{j,\tau_{1}}(\nu)\geqslant t\}$ . From the definition of $P_{j,\tau}$ in Lemma 4.2 we thus have for $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]$ and $0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau$ that

$$ P_{j,\tau}(t)\geqslant P_{j,\tau_{1}}(t). $$

For convenience, set $P_{j}(t)=P_{j,\tau_{1}}(t)$ and $R_{\beta}(t)=R_{\beta,\tau_{1}}(t)$ . It then suffices to prove that

$$ \displaystyle F(t):=P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)-t>\varepsilon^{10} $$

for all $0\leqslant t\leqslant\tau_{1}$ .

Since $\nu$ takes values in the interval $[\varepsilon^{6},\varepsilon^{-1}]$ , we can conclude the above inequality when $t$ is rather small. Indeed, for all $t\in[0,\tau_{1}]$ one has

$$ P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t)\geqslant(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3})\varepsilon^{6}=\varepsilon^{6}. $$

Thus, for $t\leqslant\varepsilon^{6}/2$ , we have

$$ F(t)\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon^{6}}{2}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

Let us assume below that $\varepsilon^{6}/2<t\leqslant\tau_{1}$ . From the definition of $R_{\beta}(t)$ , it is immediate that if $\mathcal{K}(\beta_{2},\nu;\tau_{1})\geqslant t$ and $\mathcal{K}(2\beta_{2},\nu;\tau_{1})\geqslant t$ , then $\beta_{2}\nu\geqslant R_{\beta_{2}}(t)$ and $2\beta_{2}\nu\geqslant R_{2\beta_{2}}(t)$ . Thus it follows from the definitions of $P_{2}(t)$ in Lemma 4.2 and $R_{\beta}(t)$ in (8.1) that

$$ \displaystyle P_{2}(t)\geqslant\max\left\{R_{\beta_{2}}(t),\frac{1}{2}R_{2\beta_{2}}(t)\right\}. $$

Similarly,

$$ \displaystyle P_{3}(t)\geqslant\max\left\{R_{\beta_{3}}(t),\frac{1}{2}R_{2\beta_{3}}(t)\right\},\qquad P_{1}(t)\geqslant\max\left\{\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4},\frac{1}{2}R_{2\beta_{1}}(t)\right\}. $$

We shall prove (8.6) for $t\in[\varepsilon^{6}/2,\tau_{1}]$ using these piecewise-linear lower bounds.

We first make a preliminary reduction. By (8.8), (8.7) and (8.1), we have, for $\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\leqslant\tau_{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P_{1}(t)+P_{2}(t)+P_{3}(t) \displaystyle\geqslant\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4}+\min\left\{\frac{t}{4},\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{2}}{4}\right\}+\frac{t-\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2} \displaystyle=\min\left\{t-\frac{3}{4}\tau_{1}+\frac{\beta_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}+t-\tau_{1}\right\}. $$

The second term in the minimum is $t+3/70+\varepsilon>t+\varepsilon^{10}$ . The first term is strictly greater than $t+\varepsilon^{10}$ if

$$ \beta_{1}+\beta_{3}>\frac{3}{2}\tau_{1}+2\varepsilon^{10}\iff\beta_{2}<1-\frac{3}{2}\tau_{1}-2\varepsilon^{10}. $$

Thus, using also the symmetry between $\beta_{2}$ and $\beta_{3}$ , we may restrict ourselves to the case

$$ \beta_{2},\beta_{3}\in\left[1-\frac{3}{2}\tau_{1}-2\varepsilon^{10},\tau_{1}\right]\subseteq[11/35+\varepsilon,\tau_{1}]. $$

In particular, after interchanging $\beta_{2}$ and $\beta_{3}$ if necessary, we assume from now on that

$$ \frac{11}{35}+\varepsilon\leqslant\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}\leqslant\tau_{1}. $$

Since $\varepsilon\in(0,1/100)$ , we have $11/35+\varepsilon\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ , so $\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ in this range. When $\beta\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ let

$$ \displaystyle p(\beta)=\beta-\tau_{1}/2 $$

denote the first breakpoint of (8.3) and (8.4), thus the end of the initial slope- $1/2$ segment. Similarly let

$$ \displaystyle r(\beta)=\begin{cases}\tau_{1}-2\beta/5,\qquad&\text{ if }\beta\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6;\\
3\tau_{1}/2-\beta,&\text{ if }5\tau_{1}/6\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau_{1},\end{cases} $$

denote the last breakpoint of (8.2), (8.3) and (8.4), thus the beginning of the final slope- $1/2$ segment. Then $r(\beta)$ is a continuous and non-increasing function in $\beta$ . Since $R_{\beta_{2}}(t)=R_{\beta_{3}}(t)=t/2$ whenever $0\leqslant t\leqslant p(\beta_{2})\leqslant p(\beta_{3})$ , we then have

$$ F(t)\geqslant P_{1}(t)\geqslant\beta_{1}\varepsilon^{6}\geqslant\varepsilon^{7}>\varepsilon^{10}, $$

as desired.

It therefore remains to consider the case $p(\beta_{2})\leqslant t\leqslant\tau_{1}$ . We divide the rest of the argument into two cases depending on whether $\beta_{1}\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ or $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ .

Case 1: $\beta_{1}\geqslant\tau_{1}/2$ . Define

$$ F_{+}(t)=R_{\beta_{2}}(t)+R_{\beta_{3}}(t)+\frac{t-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4}-t. $$

From (8.7)–(8.8), it suffices to show that $F_{+}(t)>\varepsilon^{10}$ whenever $t\in[p(\beta_{2}),\tau_{1}]$ . We shall show that $F_{+}(t)$ attains its minimum at $t=r(\beta_{2})$ .

When $t\in[p(\beta_{2}),r(\beta_{2})]$ , the slope of $R_{\beta_{2}}$ is at most $1/4$ , and the slope of $R_{\beta_{3}}$ is at most $1/2$ . Therefore the slope of $F_{+}(t)$ is at most $0$ . On the other hand, when $t\geqslant r(\beta_{2})\geqslant r(\beta_{3})$ both $R_{\beta_{2}}$ and $R_{\beta_{3}}$ are on their final branches (noting $r(\beta)$ is non-increasing), hence both of them have slope $1/2$ . Thus in this range $F_{+}$ has slope

$$ 1/2+1/2+1/4-1=1/4\geqslant 0. $$

Consequently, $F_{+}$ attains its minimum at $r(\beta_{2})$ , and the minimum is

$$ \displaystyle F_{+}(r(\beta_{2})) \displaystyle=\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{2}}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}}{4}-r(\beta_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{r(\beta_{2})}{4}-\frac{5}{4}\tau_{1}+\frac{1}{2}. $$

If $\beta_{2}\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ , then $r(\beta_{2})=\tau_{1}-2\beta_{2}/5$ and therefore,

$$ F_{+}(r(\beta_{2}))=-\tau_{1}-\frac{\beta_{2}}{10}+\frac{1}{2}\geqslant\frac{1}{2}-\frac{13\tau_{1}}{12}>\varepsilon^{10}, $$

If instead $\beta_{2}>5\tau_{1}/6$ , then $r(\beta_{2})=\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-\beta_{2}$ . Using also $\beta_{2}\leqslant(1-\beta_{1})/2\leqslant 1/2-\tau_{1}/4$ , we obtain

$$ F_{+}(r(\beta_{2}))=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{7\tau_{1}}{8}-\frac{\beta_{2}}{4}\geqslant\frac{3}{8}-\frac{13\tau_{1}}{16}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

This proves (8.6) in Case 1.

Case 2: $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ . Define

$$ F_{-}(t)=R_{\beta_{2}}(t)+R_{\beta_{3}}(t)+R_{2\beta_{1}}(t)/2-t. $$

For $t\in[p(\beta_{2}),r(\beta_{2})]$ , the slopes of $R_{\beta_{2}}$ , $R_{\beta_{3}}$ , and $R_{2\beta_{1}}/2$ are at most $1/4$ , $1/2$ , and $1/4$ , respectively, so the slope of $F_{-}$ is $\leqslant 0$ in this interval. For $t\in[r(\beta_{2}),\tau_{1}]$ , the first two slopes equal $1/2$ and the slope of $R_{2\beta_{1}}$ is non-negative, so the slope of $F_{-}$ is $\geqslant 0$ in this interval. Therefore $F_{-}$ attains its minimum at $r(\beta_{2})$ , and the minimum is

$$ \displaystyle F_{-}(r(\beta_{2})) \displaystyle=\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{2}}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_{2})-\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}}{2}+\frac{R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))}{2}-r(\beta_{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\beta_{1}}{2}-\tau_{1}+\frac{R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))}{2}. $$

Thus it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))>2\tau_{1}+\beta_{1}-1+2\varepsilon^{10} $$

Consider this for a fixed $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ . Now $R_{2\beta_{1}}(t)$ is increasing in $t$ while $r(\beta_{2})$ is decreasing in $\beta_{2}$ . Thus $R_{2\beta_{1}}(r(\beta_{2}))$ is minimal when $\beta_{2}$ is maximal. Since $\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}$ and $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\beta_{3}=1$ , we have $\beta_{2}\leqslant(1-\beta_{1})/2$ . Thus it suffices to show (8.11) for $\beta_{2}=(1-\beta_{1})/2$ . For $\beta_{1}<\tau_{1}/2$ , we have $(1-\beta_{1})/2\geqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ . Thus, by definition of $r(\beta)$ it suffices to show that

$$ H(\beta_{1}):=R_{2\beta_{1}}\left(\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}\right)-(2\tau_{1}+\beta_{1}-1+2\varepsilon^{10})>0. $$

Looking carefully at (8.2), (8.3), (8.4), (8.5), we see that the slope of $H(\beta_{1})$ is $\leqslant 0$ when the argument of $R_{2\beta_{1}}$ is $<r(2\beta_{1})$ and $\geqslant 0$ when the argument of $R_{2\beta_{1}}$ is $\geqslant r(2\beta_{1})$ . Thus it suffices to consider the case

$$ \frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}=r(2\beta_{1}) $$

If we had $2\beta_{1}\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ , it would follow that

$$ r(2\beta_{1})=\tau_{1}-\frac{4\beta_{1}}{5}. $$

In this case

$$ \frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}-r(2\beta_{1})=\frac{\tau_{1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{13}{10}\beta_{1}\leqslant\frac{25}{24}\tau_{1}-\frac{1}{2}<0. $$

Thus (8.13) does not have a solution with $2\beta_{1}\leqslant 5\tau_{1}/6$ and $H(\beta_{1})$ is non-increasing in this range.

For $2\beta_{1}>5\tau_{1}/6$ , by the definition of $r(\beta)$ ,

$$ \frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\beta_{1}-1}{2}=\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-2\beta_{1}\iff\beta_{1}=\frac{1}{5} $$

and

$$ R_{2/5}\left(\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}+\frac{\frac{1}{5}-1}{2}\right)=\frac{\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-\frac{2}{5}-\tau_{1}+\frac{2}{5}}{2}=\frac{\tau_{1}}{4}. $$

Thus

$$ H(1/5)=\frac{\tau_{1}}{4}-(2\tau_{1}+\frac{1}{5}-1+2\varepsilon^{10})=-\frac{7\tau_{1}}{4}+\frac{4}{5}-2\varepsilon^{10}. $$

Recalling $\tau_{1}=16/35-\varepsilon$ , we see that $H(1/5)=\frac{7}{4}\varepsilon-2\varepsilon^{10}>0$ and the claim follows. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Set $\tau^{*}=2/5-\varepsilon$ and, for convenience, set $P_{\beta}(t)=P_{\beta,\tau^{\ast}}(t)$ and $R_{\beta}(t)=R_{\beta,\tau^{\ast}}(t)$ . Arguing as in the beginning of the proof of Lemma 4.2, it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle F(t):=P_{\beta_{1}}(t)+P_{\beta_{2}}(t)+P_{\beta_{3}}(t)-t>\varepsilon^{10} $$

for all $t\in[\varepsilon^{6}/2,\tau^{\ast}]$ . Note that, for all $\beta\in\{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}\}$ ,

$$ P_{\beta}(t)\geqslant\max\Big\{R_{\beta}(t),\frac{R_{2\beta}(t)}{2}\Big\}. $$

We may assume that $\beta_{2}\leqslant\beta_{3}$ . Since $\beta_{2}\geqslant 1/5$ and $\beta_{1}\geqslant 2/5$ , we have $\beta_{1},2\beta_{2}\geqslant\tau^{*}$ . We therefore deduce from (8.15) and the definition of $R_{\beta}(t)$ that

$$ P_{\beta_{1}}(t)\geqslant R_{\beta_{1}}(t)=\frac{t}{2}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad P_{\beta_{2}}(t)\geqslant\frac{R_{2\beta_{2}}(t)}{2}=\frac{t}{4}. $$

Therefore,

$$ P_{\beta_{1}}(t)+P_{\beta_{2}}(t)+P_{\beta_{3}}(t)-t\geqslant P_{\beta_{3}}(t)-\frac{t}{4}\geqslant R_{\beta_{3}}(t)-\frac{t}{4}. $$

The remaining task is to prove that for all $t\in[\varepsilon^{6}/2,\tau^{*}]$ we have

$$ \displaystyle R_{\beta_{3}}(t)-\frac{t}{4}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

First of all, we notice that

$$ \beta_{3}\geqslant(1-\beta_{1})/2\geqslant 1/4\geqslant\tau^{*}/2. $$

If $R_{\beta_{3}}(t)=t/2$ , then (8.16) is immediate. In particular we can concentrate on the range $\beta_{3}\in[1/4,\tau^{\ast}].$ Looking at the slopes of $R_{\beta}(t)$ in (8.3) and (8.4), we see that the left-hand side of (8.16) is minimal when $t=r(\beta_{3})$ with

$$ \displaystyle r(\beta)=\begin{cases}\tau^{\ast}-2\beta/5,\qquad&\text{ if }\beta\leqslant 5\tau^{\ast}/6;\\
3\tau^{\ast}/2-\beta,&\text{ if }5\tau^{\ast}/6\leqslant\beta\leqslant\tau^{\ast},\end{cases} $$

and

$$ R_{\beta_{3}}(r(\beta_{3}))-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{r(\beta_{3})-\tau^{\ast}+\beta_{3}}{2}-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{r(\beta_{3})-2\tau^{\ast}+2\beta_{3}}{4}. $$

Now, for $\beta_{3}\in[5\tau^{\ast}/6,\tau^{\ast}]$ , we obtain

$$ R_{\beta_{3}}(r(\beta_{3}))-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{\beta_{3}-\tau^{\ast}/2}{4}\geqslant\frac{\tau^{\ast}}{12}>\varepsilon^{10}. $$

and for $\beta_{3}\in[1/4,5\tau^{\ast}/6]$ , we obtain

$$ R_{\beta_{3}}(r(\beta_{3}))-\frac{r(\beta_{3})}{4}=\frac{-\tau^{*}+8\beta_{3}/5}{4}\geqslant\frac{\varepsilon}{4}>\varepsilon^{10}, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

## 9. Multiplicative functions and almost primes in short intervals

In this section we shall briefly indicate how to prove Theorems 1.5, 1.6 and 1.7. In case $H\in[X^{0.98},X]$ we split the interval $(X,X+H]$ into intervals of length $X^{0.9}$ and apply the result with this $H$ for each subinterval. Hence we can assume that $H\in[X^{19/35+\varepsilon},X^{0.98}]$ .

We may assume that $\varepsilon\in(0,1/100)$ . The discussion in [11, Section 5.1] reduces the proofs of Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 to comparison estimates of the form (7.6). The resulting dyadic components contain a bounded number of factors with divisor-bounded coefficients, allowing fixed powers of $\log X$ . Every factor of length greater than $(2X)^{1/20}$ is an interval sum weighted by a Dirichlet character of bounded modulus, possibly with a logarithmic weight.

The proof of Proposition 7.2 extends to these components, since the extra short factors satisfy the same divisor moment bounds, and $S-2\tau>1/20$ guarantees that the singleton in case (iii) is a character-weighted interval factor. Case (i) uses periodicity and partial summation, case (ii) uses the character-weighted prime polynomial estimate, and case (iii) uses Lemma 4.1 with a character weight. This yields Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 whenever $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant Y$ .

We now turn our attention to Theorem 1.7. Take $k=100$ and write $P=\exp((\log\log X)^{2})$ and $Q=X^{\varepsilon}$ . Note that, as will become transparent later, we deliberately chose a different $k$ from the one taken in [11, Section 5.2]. Consider

$$ P(s)=\sum_{P_{1}<p\leqslant\min\{2P_{1},Q\}}p^{-s},\ \ \ \ \ \ \ N_{i}(s)=\sum_{N_{i}<n\leqslant 2N_{i}}a_{i}(n)n^{-s}, $$

where $P_{1}N_{1}\ldots N_{2k}\asymp X$ , $P_{1}\in[P,Q]$ , $N_{i}\geqslant 1/2$ , and

$$ a_{i}(n)\equiv\begin{cases}1\ \text{ or }\log n\ \text{ or }1_{n=1},&\text{if }i\leqslant k,\\[4.0pt]
\mu(n)1_{n\leqslant(2X)^{1/k}}\ \text{ or }\ 1_{n=1},&\text{if }k+1\leqslant i\leqslant 2k.\end{cases} $$

The discussion in [11, Section 5.2] leading to equation (5.7) reduces matters to showing that

$$ \int_{T_{0}}^{T_{1}}\Big\lvert P\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)N_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\ldots N_{2k}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\Big\rvert dt\ll_{A}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

with

$$ T_{0}:=X^{0.01},\qquad T_{1}:=\frac{X^{1+\varepsilon/10}}{H}. $$

As was done in [11], we split the interval $[T_{0},T_{1}]$ into two parts, namely

$$ \mathcal{T}_{1}=\{t\in[T_{0},T_{1}]:\lvert P(1/2+it)\rvert>P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-10A}X\} $$

and its complement $\mathcal{T}_{2}=[T_{0},T_{1}]\setminus\mathcal{T}_{1}$ . In order to estimate the contribution coming from $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ we follow the same procedure that was taken in the course of the proof of Proposition 7.2 to deduce (7.8), the only difference being that the bound $\lvert P(1/2+it)\rvert\leqslant P_{1}^{1/2}\log^{-10A}X$ stemming from the definition of $\mathcal{T}_{2}$ should replace the estimate (7.11) utilised there.

For the integral

$$ \int_{\mathcal{T}_{1}}\Big\lvert P\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)N_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\ldots N_{2k}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\Big\rvert dt\ll_{A}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}, $$

we consider two cases. Suppose first that $N_{i}\leqslant(2X)^{1/k}$ for all $i\leqslant 2k$ . Then, recalling that $k=100$ one may make a partition $\{1,\ldots 2k\}=\{j_{0}\}\sqcup J_{1}\sqcup J_{2}$ with $M_{1}:=\prod_{j\in J_{1}}N_{j}\in[X^{0.48},X^{1/2}]$ , and $M_{2}:=\prod_{j\in J_{2}}N_{j}\in[X^{0.48},X^{0.52}]$ and $N_{j_{0}}\geqslant X^{1/1000}$ . One then follows the procedure in the proof of Case 2.1 of Proposition 7.2 to get (9.1) by employing the pointwise bound $N_{j_{0}}(1/2+it)\ll N_{j_{0}}^{1/2}\log^{-A}X$ stemming from [10, Lemma 3.9] and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to the Dirichlet polynomials $\prod_{j\in J_{1}}N_{j}(1/2+it)$ and $\prod_{j\in J_{2}}N_{j}(1/2+it)$ . It is worth noting that in order to get the desired estimate, one should have

$$ \frac{P_{1}^{1/2}N_{j_{0}}^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}(T_{1}+M_{1})^{1/2}(T_{1}+M_{2})^{1/2}\ll\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{A}X}. $$

This holds in particular when $M_{1},M_{2}\geqslant T_{1}$ which is the case for us.

If instead there is some $j_{0}\leqslant 2k$ for which $N_{j_{0}}>(2X)^{1/k}$ then either $a_{j_{0}}(n)=1$ or $a_{j_{0}}(n)=\log n.$ Therefore, one can combine Weyl’s method to estimate $N_{j_{0}}(1/2+it)$ and the bound $\lvert\mathcal{T}_{1}\rvert\ll X^{o(1)}$ to derive (9.1) (see [11, Section 5.2] for further details).
